plain_english_point: Annual reports are maps of bottlenecks.
detailed_takeaway: Read together, the annual reports show where money, power, labor, inventory, care, infrastructure, digital trust, and consumer confidence are getting stuck. The strongest companies in this package are not just selling goods or services; they organize scarce functions that other people and institutions struggle to handle alone.
key_examples: Power, capital platforms, industrial uptime, healthcare access, built-environment upkeep, digital control, value retail
what_it_supports: A broad essay about economic bottlenecks and burden transfer
what_it_does_not_support: A stock recommendation or full proof that every company earns durable returns

plain_english_point: Power is becoming a gatekeeper for growth.
detailed_takeaway: Electricity demand matters only when it can become generated, transmitted, delivered, contracted, financed, approved, billed, and recovered. The power chapter is the strongest opening because it connects AI/data-center demand to hard infrastructure, customer obligations, utility capital plans, regulatory recovery, contractors, suppliers, and cash-proof limits.
key_examples: Constellation, Vistra, NRG, Exelon, Duke, AEP, NextEra/FPL, Sterling, MasTec
what_it_supports: A claim that power scarcity is a real operating and capital bottleneck
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that all load has been billed, collected, recovered, or converted into project returns

plain_english_point: Big asset managers are money-routing systems.
detailed_takeaway: BlackRock, Blackstone, Apollo/Athene, KKR/Global Atlantic, Brookfield, Ares, and Carlyle matter because they connect savings pools, insurance liabilities, wealth clients, institutions, credit funds, BDCs, private funds, infrastructure vehicles, and legal entities to assets and borrowers. The right question is not how large AUM is; it is where the money goes and what cash comes back.
key_examples: BlackRock, Blackstone, Apollo/Athene, KKR/Global Atlantic, Brookfield, Ares, Carlyle
what_it_supports: A bounded claim that capital platforms route money into assets, borrowers, credit, insurance portfolios, and infrastructure
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that AUM proves borrower receipts, waterfalls, or realized asset returns
writing_use: Use as financing chapter and proof discipline anchor

plain_english_point: Physical work depends on hidden access systems.
detailed_takeaway: Factories, contractors, utilities, data-center builders, HVAC technicians, and maintenance teams need equipment, parts, branches, technical support, and project execution. Industrial uptime companies are paid because work stops when these things fail.
key_examples: United Rentals, Fastenal, WESCO, Grainger, Applied Industrial, MSC Industrial, Watsco, Sterling, MasTec
what_it_supports: A claim that industrial access and uptime are real operating bottlenecks
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that sales, branch count, fleet value, or backlog proves cash collection or ROIC

plain_english_point: Demand is obvious; organized access is scarce.
detailed_takeaway: Healthcare is not scarce because people lack need. It is scarce because access, reimbursement, provider capacity, pharmacy routing, labor, authorizations, claims, home care, and trust are hard to coordinate. Healthcare companies are paid when they turn that complexity into an operating system.
key_examples: UnitedHealth, Cigna, DaVita, Option Care, Addus, BrightSpring, Enhabit
what_it_supports: A reader-friendly claim about healthcare access as burden-transfer infrastructure
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that scale proves quality, trust, reimbursement strength, or cash collection
writing_use: Use as human-centered chapter with explicit proof caveats

plain_english_point: Housing and infrastructure are upkeep systems, not one housing cycle.
detailed_takeaway: Expensive shelter and aging civic assets shift spending toward repair, replacement, waterworks, coatings, Pro channels, builder productivity, materials, HVAC, plumbing, and contractor workflows. This theme is stronger when split into sub-lanes rather than treated as a generic housing bet.
key_examples: Home Depot, Lowe's, Builders FirstSource, Sherwin-Williams, West Fraser, Ferguson, Core & Main
what_it_supports: A claim that upkeep, repair, replacement, and civic systems create durable demand channels
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that all housing exposure has the same economics or that project returns are proven

plain_english_point: Digital growth creates permission and trust bottlenecks.
detailed_takeaway: As activity moves online and AI grows, someone has to route traffic, block threats, verify users, govern participation, secure workloads, execute code, and manage digital infrastructure. The theme is not generic software growth; it is control over digital bottlenecks.
key_examples: Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, Zscaler, Fortinet, DigitalOcean, Roblox
what_it_supports: A claim that digital control points matter as online activity grows
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that ARR, RPO, traffic, bookings, or users prove durable operating leverage
writing_use: Use as digital control chapter with metrics boundary

plain_english_point: Pressured consumers split the wallet by job.
detailed_takeaway: Households under pressure do not simply trade down. They choose formats that reduce different kinds of regret: price regret, time regret, access regret, quality regret, status regret, missed-deal regret, and convenience regret.
key_examples: Costco, Walmart, Target, Dollar General, Dollar Tree, Burlington, Ollie's
what_it_supports: A claim that value retail is about consumer jobs and regret management
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that traffic, comps, membership, or gross margin proves durable cohort quality

plain_english_point: Growth only matters if it becomes cash.
detailed_takeaway: Revenue can grow while cash gets trapped in receivables, inventory, reserves, supplier finance, or poor margin quality. The working-capital box is the discipline that stops the article from equating growth with economic value.
key_examples: Target, Zebra, MSC Industrial, Global Industrial, Pool, Core Main, Arrow, Synchrony
what_it_supports: A method for evaluating whether growth is cash-realizing or cash-consuming
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that the current article has completed all receivable and inventory proof
writing_use: Use as proof box and reader method

plain_english_point: Bought scale and backlog must convert.
detailed_takeaway: Acquisitions, rollups, and backlog sound strong until they are tested against funding source, purchase accounting, backlog burn, cancellation terms, retainage, margin, collections, and debt service. Backlog is not cash.
key_examples: Sterling, MasTec, URI/Yak, Core Main, Relation, MAI, Frontline, Atwell
what_it_supports: A method for testing whether bought scale converts after close
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that transaction size or backlog proves value creation
writing_use: Use as proof box and overclaim guardrail

plain_english_point: Refinancing can help or merely move risk forward.
detailed_takeaway: A refinancing is a clean money-movement event because new cash pays off old obligations. But value depends on fees, tax, coupon change, maturity extension, liquidity, covenant cushion, settlement mechanics, and NPV, not just principal raised or redeemed.
key_examples: PBF, Matador, Devon, Liberty Broadband, Verizon, Wheaton
what_it_supports: A method for separating liquidity relief from value creation
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that refinancing automatically improves economics
writing_use: Use as proof box and capital-stack discipline

plain_english_point: Full proof needs the whole chain.
detailed_takeaway: The hard proof standard remains: source of money, wrapper, destination, use, output, cash receipt, legal claim, waterfall, and return. Most themes are article-ready before they are full named-cash-proof-ready.
key_examples: FPL, Apollo/Athene, KKR/Global Atlantic, Ares/Frontline, URI, Sterling, MasTec, Cheniere
what_it_supports: A clear boundary between synthesis writing and proof-complete claims
what_it_does_not_support: A claim that the broad article proves every dollar end to end
writing_use: Use as final caveat and future-work appendix

plain_english_point: The synthesis package is complete enough to write from.
detailed_takeaway: The project now has a thesis, theme map, chapter spines, final draft, exhibit package, source-note package, citation controls, overclaim review, theme expansion review, selection work order, and first power proof work order. That is enough to stop expanding and start writing.
key_examples: Final draft, exhibit package, publication readiness review, source lists, work orders
what_it_supports: A final bounded article and detailed theme/subtheme writing
what_it_does_not_support: External publication without citation completion or full cash-proof claims

plain_english_point: Further proof is optional and should be separate.
detailed_takeaway: Future digs can continue, but they should be treated as appendices or separate deep dives: FPL receipts, insurance statutory named income, asset-backed collateral, private-credit borrower facilities, infrastructure project cash, healthcare reimbursement, industrial uptime cash, and citation completion.
key_examples: Power/grid customer cash, insurance/statutory income, collateral, borrower facilities, healthcare reimbursement
what_it_supports: A roadmap for later proof work
what_it_does_not_support: A reason to delay writing the current synthesis forever

detailed_takeaway: The right stopping point is a bounded synthesis: annual reports reveal economic bottlenecks and the companies paid to manage them. The article can be written now, as long as it does not claim full named-cash proof for every theme.
key_examples: Seven chapters plus three proof boxes
what_it_supports: A detailed no-background-required wrap-up article and theme package
